summary: Defines a profile for X.509 Attribute Certificates for authorization. It was replaced by RFC 5755.

plainLanguage.summary: A normal certificate says who you are. This kind says what you are allowed to do. It has been replaced by RFC 5755.

questions: what is the difference between a certificate and an attribute certificate
subtitle: A certificate for saying what someone is allowed to do

tldr.problem: Public key certificates identify who someone is, but do not say what they are allowed to do. Authorization information often has a different lifetime than identity and comes from a different authority.
tldr.mechanism: Attribute certificates are separate structures that bind authorization attributes (such as group membership, role, or clearance) to an identity, digitally signed by an authority issuer rather than a certification authority.
tldr.outcome: Applications can make access control decisions based on the attributes in the certificate rather than just the identity. This has been superseded by RFC 5755.

today: RFC 3281 was a Proposed Standard published in April 2002. It has been obsoleted by RFC 5755, which updated the attribute certificate profile to align with later X.509 standards.

sections.title: Attribute Certificates for Authorization
sections.content:
An X.509 public key certificate binds an identity to a public key, much like a passport binds an identity to a photo. An attribute certificate (AC) binds authorization information to an identity without including a public key, more like a visa or badge that says what the holder is allowed to do.

Attribute certificates exist because authorization information often has a shorter lifetime than identity information and may come from a different authority. If authorization were stored in a public key certificate, the certificate would need to be reissued every time the holder's role or group membership changed, which is inefficient. By separating authorization into its own certificate, the identity certificate can remain stable while authorization certificates are issued and revoked independently.

An AC may hold various attributes such as group membership, role, security clearance, or other permissions. Applications use these attributes to decide whether to grant access to a resource or allow an action, in a practice called role-based access control.
sections.plainLanguage: A passport says who you are. This is like a work badge that says what you can do. You can give out new badges without updating your passport.

sections.title: Structure of an Attribute Certificate
sections.content:
An attribute certificate is a structure defined in X.509, containing a holder field (who the attributes apply to), an issuer field (the authority that issued the certificate), a serial number, a validity period, and a sequence of attributes. Unlike a public key certificate, it contains no public key.

The holder field identifies the certificate holder and may reference a public key certificate by issuer and serial number, use a name directly, or reference a cryptographic digest of a public key or certificate. The issuer field MUST contain a distinguished name and MUST use version 2 form to ensure the issuer does not have to know which public key certificate the verifier will use to check the signature.

The attributes field contains information about the holder's authorizations. Each attribute type may appear only once but can have multiple values. The RFC defines several standard attribute types including service authentication information, access identity, group, role, and clearance.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate says who it is for, who signed it, how long it is valid, and what the holder is allowed to do.

sections.title: Standard Attribute Types
sections.content:
RFC 3281 defines six standard attribute types for common authorization use cases. The group attribute carries group membership information, allowing systems to grant access based on group policies. The role attribute specifies roles assigned to the holder, such as Administrator or Editor, with an optional role authority field to distinguish between the same role name defined by different organizations.

The clearance attribute carries security clearance and classification information, similar to those used in military or classified systems. The classification hierarchy includes unmarked, unclassified, restricted, confidential, secret, and top-secret levels. The access identity attribute identifies the holder to a server or service for authorization purposes, while the service authentication information attribute includes credentials such as username and password for legacy systems.

The charging identity attribute identifies the holder for billing purposes, which may differ from their other identities. All these attributes use defined syntaxes to ensure verifiers can interpret them consistently across different systems.
sections.plainLanguage: You can put group membership, roles like manager, security clearances, access names, and other permissions into the certificate so the server knows what to let you do.

sections.title: Validation, Revocation, and Security
sections.content:
When verifying an attribute certificate, a system must validate that the issuer's signature is correct, that the validity period includes the current time, and that the certificate has not been revoked. The revocation status can be checked using certificate revocation lists (CRLs) referenced in the certificate or through the OCSP protocol. An issuer may indicate that no revocation information will be available by including the noRevAvail extension.

The RFC includes optional features such as AC targeting, which restricts a certificate to specific servers or groups so that an unintended server will reject it. The audit identity extension allows an issuer to provide an opaque identifier for audit trails, so administrators can track behavior without directly identifying the holder. This proves useful for privacy-sensitive environments.

The specification recommends against using chains of attribute certificates (where one AC refers to another) because the complexity is significant and adoption has been limited. Conforming implementations are only required to process a single AC at a time, though validation may require checking a chain of public key certificates leading to a trusted root.
sections.plainLanguage: The system checks that the certificate is real, not expired, and not on a revocation list. It can also restrict where the certificate works and hide the holder's identity in logs.

sections.title: Push and Pull Distribution Models
sections.content:
Attribute certificates can be distributed in two ways. In the push model, the client sends its AC to the server as part of the application request. This model works well when the client's rights are assigned within their home domain and requires no additional server burden to retrieve the certificate. The server receives only the information it needs to make access decisions.

In the pull model, the client authenticates to the server, and the server retrieves the client's AC from a repository, an online issuer, or a directory service. This model can be deployed without modifying the client or client-server protocol, making it valuable in legacy environments. The pull model suits cases where the client's rights should be assigned within the server's domain rather than the client's home domain.

The RFC anticipates both models in its design and does not specify a protocol for AC distribution, leaving this to application-specific standards. This flexibility allows different systems to adopt the model best suited to their architecture and trust relationships.
sections.plainLanguage: You can either show the server your certificate when you ask for access, or let the server look up your certificate from a directory.
